subject: Biotechnology
title: Gene Editing in Human Embryos
description: A quick, practical guide to Gene Editing in Human Embryos.

hook.text: In 2018, He Jiankui edited twin human embryos with CRISPR — the world was shocked, not impressed.

buildup.text: He claimed to disable CCR5, an HIV co-receptor — intending to make the babies resistant to HIV infection.

discovery.text: The edits were incomplete and introduced unintended mutations — mosaicism meant not all cells carried the change.

twist.text: CCR5 deletion may increase susceptibility to West Nile virus — the supposed benefit came with unknown risks.

climax.text: He was sentenced to three years in prison — the scientific community declared a moratorium on heritable editing.

punchline.text: He edited humans before science was ready — ethics cannot be optional.

quiz.question: Why was He Jiankui's experiment widely condemned?
options: The CRISPR technology he used was outdated
He edited human embryos without proper safety data, consent processes, or scientific justification
The babies did not survive the editing procedure

details.summary: Gene editing in human embryos involves modifying the genome before or shortly after fertilization, with the potential to prevent inherited diseases. However, the modifications would be present in all cells and passed to future generations, raising profound safety and ethical concerns.
details.whyItMatters: Embryo editing could eliminate genetic diseases before birth but also enables heritable human modification. The 2018 He Jiankui scandal showed the technology exists but consensus holds that it is too risky and ethically fraught for clinical
takeaways: CRISPR can edit genes in human embryos but with significant off-target risks
Mosaicism means edits may not reach all cells in the developing embryo
International moratorium exists on clinical use of heritable embryo editing

faq.question: What technical problems make embryo editing unsafe currently?
faq.answer: Mosaicism occurs when editing happens after the first cell division, leaving some cells unedited. Off-target edits at unintended sites may cause cancer or other problems.

faq.question: Are there situations where embryo editing might be justified?
faq.answer: Some argue it could be justified when both parents carry dominant genetic diseases making embryo selection impossible. However, these situations are extremely rare, and alternative reproductive options usually exist. Most scientific committees recommend against clinical use until safety is proven.
